definition: A living thing. An organism has all six characteristics of life: it is built up of cells, can reproduce, takes in and releases substances, needs energy, and reacts to its surroundings.
The smallest part that is alive. All organisms are built up of cells. Most cells are so small that you need a microscope to see them.
An organism that consists of a single cell, for example a bacterium or a paramecium. That one cell has to manage everything itself — finding food, defending itself, and reproducing.
An organism built up of many cells that work together. The cells are specialized for different tasks, for example muscle cells and nerve cells.
When a cell divides and becomes two. This is how multicellular organisms grow and replace worn-out cells, and how unicellular organisms reproduce.
Many identical cells with the same task that together form a unit, for example muscle tissue or nervous tissue.
A body part built up of several different tissues and with a specific task. The heart, lungs, liver, and kidneys are examples of organs.
The cell's outer covering. It holds the cell together and acts like a gatekeeper that decides which substances may enter and leave the cell. Found in all cells.

The cell's control center. The nucleus controls the cell and contains the genetic material (DNA), which is the blueprint for everything the cell does. Found in animal and plant cells but not in bacteria.
The jelly-like fluid inside the cell, inside the cell membrane, where the organelles are located.
The cell's power plant. In the mitochondria, the energy the cell needs to live and work is released. Found in both animal and plant cells.
The cell's protein factory. Ribosomes assemble proteins, the substances that do most of the work in the body.
A rigid shell outside the cell membrane that gives the cell a fixed, angular shape and support. Found in plant cells (and bacteria) but not in animal cells.
The green organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place. Chloroplasts capture light energy from the sun. Animal cells lack chloroplasts.
A fluid-filled sac in the cell. In plant cells the vacuole is often large and central; it stores substances and gives the cell firmness.
The process in plants' chloroplasts where light energy from the sun is captured and used to build energy-rich substances. Animals cannot use light as an energy source.
The genetic material found in the cell nucleus. DNA is the blueprint that determines the characteristics of the cell and the organism. You will meet DNA again in the Genetics topic.
A unicellular organism that is much smaller than our own cells and lacks a cell nucleus. Many bacteria are useful decomposers; some cause diseases.

An infectious agent that does not consist of cells and is usually not considered alive. A virus is a shell containing genetic material that must hijack a living cell in order to reproduce. Antibiotics do not help against viruses.
Organisms, for example bacteria and fungi, that break down dead plants and animals into nutrients that become new soil.
Medicines, for example penicillin, that kill or inhibit bacteria. Antibiotics only work against bacteria — not against viruses. They should be used sparingly so as not to create resistant bacteria.
A group of organisms that can produce fertile offspring together under natural conditions — offspring that can in turn have offspring of their own. Humans are a species (Homo sapiens).
A mix between two different species, for example a mule (horse × donkey). Hybrids are often infertile and therefore cannot have offspring themselves.
The largest classification of all living things. The three domains are true bacteria, archaea, and organisms with a cell nucleus (plants, fungi, and animals).
